article.title: How to Caulk Exterior Windows (and Stop Drafts)
article.summary: Caulk exterior windows to stop drafts and water: remove old caulk, fill wide gaps with backer rod, lay a smooth bead and keep weep holes open.
article.body:
Cracked or missing caulk around the outside of a window lets in drafts, water and insects. Recaulking is a cheap, high-value job you can do in an afternoon. This guide covers the joint between the window trim and the siding or brick.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: follow ladder safety rules for upper windows: set the base on firm, level ground and keep three points of contact. If your home was built before 1978, old paint on window trim may contain lead; avoid dry-sanding or scraping it heavily without lead-safe precautions.

Steps

  1. Pick dry weather and the right sealant

    Choose a dry day within the temperature range on the label, often about 40 to 90°F. Use an exterior sealant made for windows and doors: polyurethane or hybrid sealants grip well and can be painted, and 100% silicone lasts long but usually can't be painted.

    Done right: no rain is due for 24 hours and your sealant is rated for exterior windows.

  2. Remove old, failing caulk

    Cut along both edges of the old bead with a utility knife and pull or scrape it out with a putty knife. Remove anything cracked, loose or shrunken; caulk that's still firmly bonded can stay if you're caulking over the same type.

    Done right: the joint is clear of loose or cracked caulk.

  3. Clean and fill deep gaps

    Brush out dirt and wipe the joint with rubbing alcohol. Press foam backer rod into any gap wider than about 1/4 in, so the caulk bead isn't too deep. A good joint is about as deep as it is wide.

    Done right: the joint is clean and dry, and deep gaps are filled with backer rod to about 1/4 in from the surface.

  4. Lay a steady bead

    Cut the tube nozzle at a 45-degree angle to make a hole slightly smaller than the gap. Push the bead ahead of the nozzle in one steady pass along each side. Tool it smooth with a wet finger or a caulk tool, pressing it into both surfaces.

    Done right: the bead is smooth, continuous and bonded to both the trim and the siding.

  5. Leave weep holes and drainage paths open

    Many windows have small weep holes or slots in the bottom of the frame that let water drain out. Don't caulk over them. Also leave the joint under a drip cap open if the window was built to drain there.

    Done right: every weep hole and drainage gap is still open.

Call a window or siding pro if: trim or the window sill is soft or rotted, water stains show inside around the window, or the window frame itself is cracked. Caulk won't fix rot or failed flashing.

FAQ

What kind of caulk is best for exterior windows?

An exterior window and door sealant: polyurethane or hybrid sealants for paintable joints, or 100% silicone where you won't paint.

Should you caulk the bottom of a window?

Caulk the trim to the siding, but never block the weep holes in the bottom of the window frame, which let water drain out.

How often should exterior window caulk be replaced?

Check it every year or two. Replace it when it cracks, shrinks or pulls away, often every 5 to 10 years depending on the product and exposure.

Can you caulk over old caulk?

Only if the old caulk is firmly bonded and the same type. Cracked or loose caulk should come out first.
